'''Canary grass''' is a plant, '''''Phalaris canariensis''''', belonging to the family [[Poaceae]].  Originally a native of the [[Mediterranean]] region, it is now grown commercially in several parts of the world for birdseed.

== Description ==
''Phalaris canariensis'' resembles ''[[Phalaris arundinacea]]'' (reed canary grass), a perennial forage crop and a wild grass. Although heads of both crops are panicles, ''Phalaris canariensis'' heads resemble club wheat. This large, coarse grass has erect, hairless stems, usually from {{convert|2 to 6|ft|m}} tall. The [[ligule]] is prominent and membranous, {{convert|1/4|in|cm}} long and rounded at the apex. The gradually tapering leaf blades are {{convert|3+1/2 to 10|in|cm}} long, {{convert|1/4 to 3/4|in|cm}} wide, flat, and often harsh on both surfaces.  The compact [[panicles]] are erect or sometimes slightly spreading and range from {{convert|3 to 16|in|cm}} long with branches {{convert|1/2 to 1+1/2|in|cm}} long. Single flowers occur in dense clusters in May to mid-June or August. [[Inflorescence]]s are green or slightly purple at first, then become tan.

== Seeds ==

The seeds are shiny brown. The seed is used as [[bird food]] and is generally mixed with [[rapeseed]] and other seeds that cheapen it. It should be kept in a dry place and away from vermin. Industrially, a flour made from seed is employed in the manufacture of fine cotton goods and silk stuffs.

In the [[Canary Islands]], [[Italy]] and [[North Africa]], ''Phalaris canariensis'' is used as food. In certain parts of [[Mexico]], such as [[Valle de Bravo]], it is prepared and sold by [[street food]] vendors as a much appreciated form of [[atole]]. However, the seed hulls appear to contain [[silica]] fibers, which are linked to [[esophageal cancer]].<ref name="Craddock1993-p202">{{cite book|author=Valda M. Craddock|title=Cancer of the Esophagus: Approaches to the Etiology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OS89AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA202|year=1993|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-37393-7|pages=202}}</ref> In 2013, a new hull-less or [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] variety was announced as a [[Gluten-free diet|gluten-free food]] for humans.<ref>Joyce Irene Boye, Alloua Achouri, Nancy Raymond, Chantal Cleroux, Dorcas Weber, Terence B. Koerner, Pierre Hucl, Carol Ann Patterson, "Analysis of Glabrous Canary Seeds by ELISA, Mass Spectrometry, and Western Blotting for the Absence of Cross-Reactivity with Major Food Plant Allergens", ''Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry'', 2013, 130617150432002 DOI: 10.1021/jf305500t .</ref>
